title: Repeat Expansion Disorders: Fragile X, Huntington Disease, Myotonic Dystrophy
summary: Classify FMR1, HTT and DMPK repeat sizes, explain anticipation and parent-of-origin expansion, and compare PCR with Southern blot for sizing repeats.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 72 Hits 1, 3, 4 and 5 and Trap 1. Checked against Maddalena 2001 (ACMG fragile X standards), Sherman 2005, Ciaccio 2017, Nopoulos 2016, Chintalaphani 2021 and Wenninger 2018. Corrections: Huntington 36–39 is reduced penetrance, not a no-disease intermediate (rv-hd-intermediate); congenital DM1 is mostly but not only maternal (rv-dm1-maternal). Not taught: “paternal transmission gives the largest expansions (juvenile onset)” beyond Nopoulos’s “expansion more likely in male transmission”, and the reviewer’s DM1 disease range “> 100” and congenital range “1000–2000”.

objectives: Classify FMR1 CGG, HTT CAG and DMPK CTG repeat sizes.
Explain anticipation and which parent transmits expansions for each disorder.
Compare PCR and Southern blot for repeat sizing and methylation.

scenes.title: Earlier every generation
scenes.altText: An invented three-generation family (schematic): grandmother with symptoms at 62, her son at 41, his daughter at 19. Each figure carries a bead bar (a repeat tract) that is longer than the one above it. Question token: “Why does the disease come earlier each generation?”

cues.text: In this invented family, the grandmother first has symptoms at 62, her son at 41, and his daughter at 19.
Look inside the gene: a short DNA motif repeated over and over. The repeat tract is longer in each generation.
Why does the disease come earlier, and how does the lab count the repeats?

props.label: Why earlier? How do we count?

scenes.title: Normal repeat tracts
scenes.altText: Three gene cards with their repeat motif and usual range: FMR1 (fragile X) CGG in the 5′ untranslated region, normal about 5–44, most often 29–30, stable from parent to child; HTT (Huntington disease) CAG, below 27 stable; DMPK (myotonic dystrophy type 1) CTG, 5–37 in healthy people. A note: anticipation = earlier onset and/or greater severity in later generations, caused by repeat instability.

cues.text: Some genes contain short tandem repeats. In FMR1, the fragile X gene, a CGG repeat sits in the untranslated start of the gene. Normal alleles have about 5 to 44 repeats, most often 29 or 30, and pass stably to children.
In HTT, the Huntington gene, a CAG repeat below 27 copies is stable and causes no disease.
In DMPK, the myotonic dystrophy type 1 gene, healthy people carry 5 to 37 CTG repeats.
Long repeats are unstable when passed on. As they grow from one generation to the next, symptoms appear earlier or more severely. That is anticipation.

props.title: Anticipation
lines: Unstable repeat grows when passed on
Earlier onset / more severe in later generations

scenes.title: When the repeat grows
scenes.altText: Three range ladders. FMR1: 45–54 gray zone; ~55–200 premutation (unmethylated, unstable); >200 full mutation — hypermethylated, gene silenced, no FMRP. Expansion to a full mutation happens through the mother; a premutation carrier father passes a premutation to his daughters, not a full mutation. HTT: 27–35 intermediate (no disease, may expand, more likely through the father); 36–39 reduced penetrance; ≥ 40 full penetrance; longer repeats → earlier onset. DMPK: 38–49 premutation; > 50 fully penetrant; congenital form usually > 1,000 CTG, characteristically from the mother.

cues.text: Fragile X: 45 to 54 is a gray zone. About 55 to 200 is a premutation, unmethylated and unstable.

Above 200, the full mutation is hypermethylated, the gene is silenced and no FMRP protein is made. Expansion to a full mutation happens through the mother; fathers pass a premutation to their daughters.
Huntington: 27 to 35 repeats cause no disease but can expand, more often through the father. 36 to 39 is reduced penetrance: some carriers get the disease. 40 or more is fully penetrant.
Longer CAG repeats mean earlier onset; very long repeats cause juvenile Huntington disease, before age 21.
Myotonic dystrophy type 1: 38 to 49 repeats is a premutation, more than 50 is fully penetrant, and the congenital form, usually over 1,000 repeats, characteristically comes from the mother.

scenes.title: Counting repeats in the lab
scenes.altText: Two method cards. PCR with flanking primers: product size gives the repeat number; precise for normal, gray-zone and premutation alleles, works on small DNA amounts with fast turnaround; but efficiency falls as repeats lengthen, so large expansions may give no product, and it gives no methylation status. Southern blot with a methylation-sensitive restriction enzyme: detects all size ranges and shows methylation, but sizing is crude, it is labor-intensive and needs more DNA. Token: laboratories need both. Token: repeat-primed PCR and long-read sequencing are also used.

cues.text: PCR uses primers on either side of the repeat. The product size gives the repeat count, precisely for normal, gray-zone and premutation alleles, from a small amount of DNA.
But PCR efficiency falls as the repeat lengthens: a large full mutation may give no product at all, and PCR says nothing about methylation.
Southern blot with a methylation-sensitive enzyme sees alleles of every size and shows whether the gene is methylated, but sizing is crude, it is slow and it needs more DNA.
So fragile X laboratories keep both methods. Repeat-primed PCR and long-read sequencing are newer options.
Back to the family: the repeat grew each generation, and the age of onset fell. That is anticipation.

props.label: Labs keep both · plus repeat-primed PCR, long reads

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Fragile X expands to a full mutation in male meiosis” (✓ expansion happens through the mother; a premutation father passes a premutation to his daughters, and his sons are not at risk); “Huntington 36–39 is a harmless intermediate range” (✓ 36–39 is reduced penetrance; 27–35 is the intermediate, non-disease range); “Congenital myotonic dystrophy is never paternal” (✓ characteristically maternal, but paternal cases are known).

cues.text: Trap one: fragile X expands to a full mutation in male meiosis. No: expansion happens through the mother. A father with a premutation passes a premutation to his daughters, and his sons are not at risk.
Trap two: 36 to 39 Huntington repeats are a harmless intermediate. No: that range has reduced penetrance. The intermediate, non-disease range is 27 to 35.
Trap three: congenital myotonic dystrophy is never paternal. It characteristically comes from the mother, but paternal cases are reported.

props.title: ✗ “Fragile X fully expands in male meiosis.”
lines: ✓ Via mother; fathers pass a premutation

scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Mom grows the X and the DM baby; Dad grows the hunt.” Tokens: Fragile X → mother; congenital DM1 → mother; Huntington → father. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: Mom grows the X and the myotonic baby; Dad grows the hunt. Fragile X and congenital myotonic dystrophy expand mostly through the mother; Huntington repeats expand more often through the father.
Where it breaks: paternal congenital myotonic dystrophy is reported; Huntington repeats can expand through either parent; the cutoffs are approximate and differ slightly between sources.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “FMR1 CGG: 45–54 gray · 55–200 pre · > 200 full (silenced) — expands via mother”, “HTT CAG: 27–35 intermediate · 36–39 reduced penetrance · ≥ 40 full · DM1 congenital mostly maternal”.

cues.text: Unstable repeats grow when passed on, causing anticipation. Fragile X expands through the mother; Huntington 36 to 39 is reduced penetrance; congenital myotonic dystrophy is mostly maternal.

props.label: FMR1 CGG: 45–54 gray · 55–200 pre · > 200 full, silenced · expands via mother
HTT CAG: 27–35 int. · 36–39 reduced pen. · ≥ 40 full · congenital DM1 mostly maternal

explanation.what: Plain language: some genes contain a short DNA motif repeated many times; if the repeat grows too long the gene fails, and long repeats tend to grow further when passed to children. Scientific terms: short tandem repeat, trinucleotide repeat expansion, premutation, full mutation, gray zone, reduced penetrance, anticipation, hypermethylation, FMRP.
explanation.why: Long repeats are unstable during transmission, so repeat length — and with it earlier onset or greater severity — increases across generations (anticipation). In fragile X, a full mutation (> 200 CGG) is hypermethylated, silencing FMR1 so no FMRP is made. Which parent transmits the allele affects how much it grows.
explanation.measure: FMR1 CGG (ACMG 2001): normal ~5–44, gray zone ~45–54, premutation ~55–200, full mutation > 200 (some sources ~230). HTT CAG (Nopoulos 2016): < 27 stable, 27–35 no disease but may expand, 36–39 incomplete penetrance, ≥ 40 full penetrance. DMPK CTG (Wenninger 2018): 5–37 healthy, 38–49 premutation, > 50 penetrant, congenital form usually > 1,000. PCR with flanking primers sizes small alleles precisely but large expansions may not amplify and it gives no methylation status; Southern blot with a methylation-sensitive enzyme detects all sizes and methylation but sizes crudely.
explanation.differs: Fragile X expands to a full mutation through the mother (fathers pass premutations to all daughters; sons not at risk); HTT expansion is more likely in male transmission; congenital DM1 is characteristically maternal. DM2 shows no anticipation.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: anticipation definition, fragile X repeat categories, which parent expands each disorder, HD penetrance ranges, and PCR vs Southern blot limits.

mnemonic.text: Mom grows the X and the DM baby; Dad grows the hunt.
mnemonic.explanation: Fragile X full mutations and congenital myotonic dystrophy arise mainly through maternal transmission; Huntington CAG expansion is more likely in paternal transmission.
mnemonic.limitation: Paternal congenital DM1 is reported; HD repeats can expand through either parent; repeat cutoffs are approximate and differ between sources.

takeaway: Unstable repeats grow when passed on and cause anticipation: fragile X expands through the mother, Huntington 36–39 CAG is reduced penetrance, and congenital myotonic dystrophy is mostly maternal.

questions.stem: A woman’s FMR1 testing shows one allele of 30 CGG repeats and one of 90, unmethylated. How is the 90-repeat allele classified?

options.rationale: Correct. About 55–200 unmethylated repeats is the premutation range; it is unstable and can expand to a full mutation in her children.
Incorrect. Full mutations exceed about 200 repeats and are hypermethylated.
Incorrect. The gray zone is about 45–54 repeats.
Incorrect. Normal alleles have about 5–44 repeats.

questions.stem: A man with an FMR1 premutation asks about risk to his children. Which statement is correct?

options.text: His daughters will almost always inherit a premutation; his sons are not at risk
options.rationale: Correct. Fathers pass the X to daughters; male transmission does not usually expand a premutation to a full mutation, and sons receive his Y.

options.text: His sons are at high risk of a full mutation
options.rationale: Incorrect. Sons inherit his Y chromosome, not his X.

options.text: His daughters will usually inherit a full mutation
options.rationale: Incorrect. Expansion to a full mutation occurs through the mother; affected daughters of premutation fathers are extremely rare.

options.text: His children are not at risk because premutations are stable
options.rationale: Incorrect. Premutations are unstable; his daughters’ children are at risk.

questions.skill: Parent of origin in fragile X

questions.stem: A sample with a suspected large fragile X full mutation shows only one normal-sized product by PCR with flanking primers. What is the best next step?

options.text: Southern blot with a methylation-sensitive enzyme
options.rationale: Correct. Large expansions may not amplify by PCR; Southern blot detects all sizes and shows methylation.
Incorrect. A large expansion can fail to amplify, so a single product does not exclude it.

options.text: Repeat the same PCR with more cycles
options.rationale: Incorrect. PCR efficiency falls with repeat length, and PCR still gives no methylation status.
Incorrect. A karyotype cannot size the repeat or show methylation.

accuracyFlags.issue: The reviewer calls HTT 36–39 CAG “intermediate”. Nopoulos 2016 and Chintalaphani 2021 classify 36–39 as reduced (incomplete) penetrance; 27–35 is the range that causes no disease but may expand. See register flag rv-hd-intermediate.
The reviewer says congenital DM1 is transmitted maternally only. Wenninger 2018: characteristically maternal, but paternal transmission is also known. See register flag rv-dm1-maternal.
Repeat cutoffs are approximate and differ between sources (e.g., full fragile X mutation > 200 or > 230; DM1 normal 5–35 vs 5–37).
